title: the one at every doorway
hook: why Hindus begin everything with Ganesha, and the tusk he broke to keep writing

segments.voice: Every Hindu beginning starts with him, so this one does too. A small statue on a taxi dashboard. A picture above a shop counter. His name printed at the top of a wedding invitation, before anyone else's. Elephant head, round belly, one tusk broken. He sits wherever things start, and that's the clue to who he is.
screen: `EVERY BEGINNING STARTS WITH HIM.` → `DASHBOARDS. DOORWAYS. INVITATIONS.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. His best-known title is Vighnaharta. Vighna, an obstacle; harta, one who removes. The remover of obstacles. This is why Hindus begin everything with Ganesha: before a wedding, a puja, a new shop, a new home or an exam, you honor first the one who clears the way. And there's a story about him and a page. When the sage Vyasa was ready to give the world the Mahabharata, he needed a scribe who could keep up. Ganesha agreed, on one condition: Vyasa must never stop. Vyasa added his own: Ganesha must understand every verse before he wrote it down. So whenever Vyasa needed time, he spoke a verse so knotted that even Ganesha had to stop and think. And one telling says that when Ganesha's pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing. That's the broken tusk in his pictures. The remover of obstacles is also a god of wisdom and learning. So some people write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before they begin. Namah means a bow: a bow to Ganesha, before the work.
screen: `VIGHNAHARTA — REMOVER OF OBSTACLES.` · `HONORED FIRST, BEFORE ANY BEGINNING.` · `VYASA SPEAKS. GANESHA WRITES.` · `THE BROKEN TUSK.` · `SHRI GANESHAYA NAMAH.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Think of something you're beginning this week. If you pray, say shri ganeshaya namah once, under your breath, the way many Hindus do before they start. If you don't, rest a hand on the door or the notebook, and name what's in the way. Then breathe out, and begin.
Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. First word on your strand, and the first name.

segments.voice: Your line: clear the road, then begin. It's why his name comes first on so many invitations, and why he came first here. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at pujas, weddings, housewarmings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, print his image or name at the top of invitations, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

story.title: the race around the world
story.text: In a story told in many versions, Shiva and Parvati offer a prize to whichever of their two sons can go around the whole world first. Kartikeya jumps on his peacock and flies off. Ganesha, round and slow, with a mouse to ride, doesn't even try to race. He walks around his parents, slowly, and bows. You two are my world, he says. He wins.
story.source: a popular story, told in different forms across India

Body symbolism (ears, eyes, belly) is given as 'a popular way of reading the body', not scripture. Confirm.
